courses.name: AWS API Gateway - Introduction
courses.title: AWS is an ocean as we all know. It feels like there's a new AWS Service that comes into existence every single day. In this course, we will take a high level look at API Gateway (Length: 32 minutes).
courses.description: Snowpal began its presence as a B2C company but with the recent launch of our APIs (6 of them, and growing!), we have officially entered the B2B space. And we couldn't be more excited about it! As part of the efforts that went into the launch of our very first API, we learned very many things but also realized one important thing: a lot of what you need to know to build APIs is not documented well. Sure, there's no dearth of documentation but good luck navigating through all of that on your own. We would be sharing a lot of our learnings in our API Gateway Course Series, the first of which is available for you to purchase now. Do not wait to get started!

descriptions: This course is a hands-on introduction to API gateways, taught from the perspective of an engineering team that recently published multiple APIs to AWS Marketplace and other hubs. Instead of abstract theory, it provides a pragmatic walkthrough of what an API gateway is, where it sits between clients and backend services, and why teams adopt one as they grow. The session remains compact and accessible while grounding every concept in real deployment scenarios. You will begin by clarifying definitions. The course compares general explanations with those offered by AWS and then anchors those ideas in a simple end-to-end diagram.

Next, the course demonstrates how Snowpal exposes APIs through channels such as AWS Marketplace, Rapid, and other hubs, and explains what this means for consumers. You will learn what a subscriber actually receives, including an API key and a product code, how Postman workspaces accelerate onboarding, and how hub URLs map to gateway endpoints behind the scenes. The result is a clear picture of consumption paths without overwhelming you with vendor-specific detail. By the end of the course, you will understand the purpose and mechanics of API gateways in a modern microservices stack.

courses.name: Manage Projects on Github
courses.title: GitHub Projects has changed quite a bit over the years. While we've used other solutions in the past for managing our issues across repos, we've come to realize the benefits of using a solution that lives smack next to our repos (Length: 37 minutes).
courses.description: Being closer to your repos makes project management a lot easier. At Snowpal, we have numerous apps in Production. And at least, 4 different environments per App (in some cases, a few more). Therefore, at any given time, we have a varied set of versions deployed across these environments. As a Project Manager (regardless of how technical you are), this can get rather challenging. A good process to manage multiple repos, multiple apps, and multiple developers is one that would hold you in good stead.

descriptions: This course takes a hands-on and real-world approach to GitHub Projects, showing you how to use it as a lightweight yet powerful project management tool that lives directly alongside your codebase. Unlike higher-level tools such as Jira or Trello, GitHub Projects sits next to your repositories, pull requests, and issues, making it a natural choice for repository-level planning and tracking. You will learn not through abstract theory but through practical examples drawn from our own production workflow. You will also walk through custom fields, views, and advanced project structuring.

You will learn how to add fields such as due dates, levels of effort, and statuses, and how to create multiple views for different roles. Developers can benefit from daily scrum boards, while project managers can rely on high-level summaries. The course also shows how projects can be organized hierarchically, with master projects spanning multiple repositories while still supporting repository-specific tracking at the developer level. Next, the course demonstrates how to connect GitHub Projects to code workflows. The course concludes with a discussion of limitations and best practices.

courses.name: Build a Website on Canva
courses.title: Canva is one of the most popular tools out there, and whether you have a team dedicated to do creative work or otherwise, you would be well served to check it out. It saves us a ton of time (Length: 43 minutes).
courses.description: There's a number of ways to build a website. Of course. There is also a myriad of tools that will help you build sites in quick time. However, a lot of them end up taking a lot of time in the long run even if they look promising at first. Besides, some of them are specifically geared towards building websites. What if you wanted to generate a quick graphic and just that? What if you wanted to create presentations that didn't look dated? (read: Powerpoint!). Well, that's where Canva as a product makes a world of a difference. The website you are looking at right now was built in under an hour. Like it? If so, purchase this course.

descriptions: This course is a fast and pragmatic tour of Canva, taught from the perspective of a builder. Instead of focusing on abstract design theory, it demonstrates how an engineering-led team at Snowpal uses Canva to produce real assets quickly, including landing pages, course sites, presentations, thumbnails, and promotional graphics. The emphasis is on speed, clarity, and creating something you can publish immediately. From there, the course focuses on building a one-page website, which is the format Canva handles especially well. Hands-on segments cover the everyday techniques that make Canva efficient.

The course also provides honest context on tooling choices. It explains how platforms such as Kajabi can be powerful but also expensive and complex, and when a streamlined Canva workflow with a relatively low annual cost is the better option. This is especially true for startups that are managing a large number of competing priorities. The goal is not to declare a single best tool but to help you create the right asset with the least amount of friction. By the end of the course, you will be able to design a cohesive one-page site, remix templates without breaking layouts, and deliver polished assets ready for your team.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.description: We'll create 3 pages based on a template.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.description: We'll add elements to pages, create animations, & reference a file attachment from box.com.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.description: Record videos, and add them inline to pages. Look at Brand Templates.

courses.name: How to use Postman API Client
courses.title: If you are building APIs, you are likely using Postman. You are also likely using it if you are consuming APIs. Let's look at some of the common Postman features you would mostly be using on a daily basis (Length: 46 minutes).
courses.description: Whether you are building APIs to monetize them directly, or to simply serve the backend needs for your Web, Mobile or Server Side Apps, using a good API client is imperative to your project's turnaround times (and therefore, your success, your team's success and your company's success). While there are quite a few options out there,  Postman is one of the most popular tools out there. it is likely you've heard of it, and it is likely you are even using it. But, are you using it well?  Are you enjoying the time you are spending on the tool, and is it serving your expectations just fine? If you are even slightly unsure, check out our course and we are quite confident it will help you use Postman better.

descriptions: This course is a fast and pragmatic introduction to using Postman as an everyday API client, taught by the engineering lead at Snowpal. It is designed as a concise hands-on walkthrough lasting between ten and twenty minutes, rather than a lecture heavy on theory. You will see exactly how a practicing team uses Postman to build, publish, and consume real APIs that are shipped on AWS Marketplace and other hubs. Snowpal uses Postman collections as living and shareable bundles of endpoints that reflect the way features such as dashboards are organized.

Next, the course walks you through building your first request in a structured way. You will define the HTTP method and the URL, beginning with a local server for speed, and then add a clear and consistent title. You will learn why small habits of naming and structure provide significant long-term benefits when a single API expands to hundreds of endpoints. You will also see how the same request can later transition to secure protocols and production hosts with minimal adjustments. By the end of the course, you will have a working Postman workspace that reflects real-world practice.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.description: Introduction to Postman API Client. We'll take a look at Collections, and Endpoints.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.description: We'll add Headers, Enviroments, and APIs. Look at how to publish APIs to Custom Domains, and a bit more.

courses.name: Flutter Mobile App - Caching
courses.title: Caching API responses allows you to reduce the number of networks calls, and make your pages render much faster (Length: 31 minutes).
courses.description: Say, your team worked real hard and built a wonderful app (one that solved real customer problems). You would be both proud and real excited to sell it. (And, why shouldn't you be!) Now, you take it to your customers and they report that the screens takes 2 to 3 seconds, on an average, to render. How would you feel? How would they feel? Your customers expect your app(s) to do what you promised in terms of functionality but they also expect it to perform well. That's a given in this day and age. And if your app makes an API request all the time, especially when it doesn't need to, it is going to slow it down, and will take everyone else's productivity along with it. But, don't you worry. I'll teach you how to implement caching on your Flutter App. It will make a world of a difference when it comes to your app's performance.

descriptions: This course is a pragmatic, hands-on walkthrough of how Snowpal implements client-side caching in its Flutter mobile application for iOS and Android. You will see how caching fits into a real product that makes numerous network calls and why optimizing those calls is essential for fast and reliable user experiences. Rather than focusing on theory, the material reflects on our production practices so that you can apply the ideas immediately. You will learn why client-side caching is vital when connectivity is poor, backend cache policies are uncontrollable, or multiple datasets must load consistently across screens.

You will then tour the working setup, which consists of a Flutter application developed in Android Studio, backed by Snowpal APIs over HTTP and HTTPS. On-device data is cached in SQLite, with each entry containing a cache key, a JSON payload, and a last modified timestamp. The course demonstrates how the team inspects and validates these entries using a database browser so that you can confidently verify what is stored. The course covers cache design and invalidation, showing how Snowpal uses targeted keys to keep entries precise and payloads small. By the end, you will have a practical blueprint to add or improve caching in your Flutter apps.

courses.name: AWS Machine Learning with No Data Science Experience
courses.title: If you have an interest in exploring Machine Learning (who doesn't?) but have no Data Science experience, you can check this course out (Length: 33 minutes).
courses.description: Machine Learning is a fascinating field and a lot of us are scratching the surface, at best. I suspect we are going to spend a lot of our lives learning and excelling at everything that is Machine Learning related in the coming years. We look forward to the challenges eagerly, and as we embark on building our first ML API in the coming quarters, we wanted to take a moment to share some of our real high level learnings with you. This is ML 101 when it comes to me taking a crack at Machine Learning but I hope it piques your interest, and clarifies a few basic questions about some of Amazon's ML Services.

descriptions: This course is a fast, practical introduction to building a machine learning powered chatbot on AWS, focused on recommendations. No prior data science expertise is required. Lessons are short (10 to 20 minutes) and emphasize hands-on steps and practical tips over theory, helping engineers get results quickly and know where to dive deeper later. You will start by preparing sample retail data, uploading provided ZIP archives to Amazon S3, and organizing resources. Workflow advice covers AWS Console best practices, including managing tabs, copying ARNs/URIs, and avoiding throttling or delays.

The course then walks you through Amazon Personalize to build recommendation models from uploaded data. You will define schemas, create dataset groups, import interactions, items, and users, then train a solution and recommender. Since training takes time, you will learn which tasks to run in parallel and how to verify readiness. The course closes with iteration tips on data quality, re-ingestion, and evolving recommendations, while showing when to rely on managed services versus deeper ML skills. You will leave with a mental model linking S3, Personalize, Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, HTML, and Lex.

courses.name: Implement Mind Map Chart (amCharts)
courses.title: If you want to display hierarchical data as a series of bubbles that are linked, a Mind Map is one of the best ways to go about it. amCharts offers a Force Directed Chart that is essentially a Mind Map (Length: 26 minutes).
courses.description: We use a variety of charts in one of our products (check out https://snowpal.com), and after assessing a number of Charting Libraries, we narrowed down on amCharts for a few different reasons. In this course, we'll take a brief look at one of the charts we love, Mind Maps. Or, as amCharts calls it, Force Directed Charts. We'll look at the JSON Data Structure required by the chart, a Mongo Aggregate Pipeline query that we wrote to extract the data from our database, and discuss a bit about the data massaging needed to render the chart.

descriptions: This course introduces AM Charts through our real-world integration in its project management platform. Instead of abstract demos, lessons show how force-directed charts (mind maps) render product data structures like keys, blocks, and pods. You will first learn the context and data model: keys as projects, blocks as major building blocks such as iOS or Android apps, and pods as subcomponents like presentation or functional layers. The course guides you in creating sample data and shows how links enable reuse across keys, building the foundation for visualizing relationships in charts.

Next, the course explores the API and JSON structure behind the visualization. You will review real API responses and see how Snowpal maps terms like blocks and pods into a normalized format for AM Charts. Server-side logic, built in Ruby with MongoDB pipelines, processes data into chart-ready form while remaining flexible for multiple front-end clients. By the end, you will know how to model data, design API responses, and format JSON for rendering, while gaining practical insight into how Snowpal solved visualization challenges you can apply to your own apps, dashboards, or reports.

courses.name: Securing Microservices in an API Gateway
courses.title: We have several microservices, and while each of them serves a unique purpose, they do have a few things in common. Security, is one of them. Therefore, we have microservices that exclusively deal with Security, and we'll take a look at one of them (Length: 32 minutes).
courses.description: At Snowpal, we have several microservices, and while each of them serves a unique purpose, they do have a few things in common. Security, is one of them. Therefore, we have microservices that exclusively deal with Security, and we'll take a look at one of them. At the end of this 20-ish minute course, the expectation is that you get a good sense of how a Microservices Security Architecture works. Whether you are breaking a monolith into a set of microservices, or are building a brand new microservice, this course should help you understand how Security Integration could work in those contexts.

descriptions: This course provides a pragmatic overview of API Gateway security by showing how Snowpal protects six production APIs. Instead of theory, lessons focus on real implementations to build a clear mental model of securing live client traffic. You will first learn the role of the gateway in our architecture: every request from mobile, web, microservices, or CLI clients passes through it before reaching backends. Positioned in the demilitarized zone, the gateway validates requests and routes them safely, ensuring no client interacts directly with internal APIs or databases.

The course then covers the three headers that secure API requests: API key, product code, and user authorization token. You will see how Snowpal issues them at subscription, why both key and code are required to validate caller and product, and how tokens generated by the security API are shared across services. By the end, you will have a blueprint for securing APIs in microservices: centralize authentication, validate headers at the gateway, and design reusable tokens. While proprietary details remain abstracted, the course gives patterns you can adapt to balance usability, maintainability, and strong security.

courses.name: Implementing Web Services in Golang
courses.title: Let's take a quick look at implementing REST endpoints in Golang using Gin Framework. We'll go over routes, services, models and make some code changes to see how they take effect (Length: 28 minutes).
courses.description: Let's take a quick look at implementing REST endpoints in Golang. We'll go over routes, services, models and make some code changes to see how they take effect. At the end of this 20-minute course, you should be able to start creating Web Services in Go. We'll be using Gin Framework for implementing these endpoints.

descriptions: This course provides a hands-on introduction to building RESTful endpoints in Go using our production APIs. You will see how services connect to persistence layers and expose secure JSON responses. Starting with the Status API, published on AWS Marketplace, you will explore its role in managing team statuses across web, mobile, Slack, and microservices. Lessons focus on user sign-in and team listing, giving a complete view of the request/response lifecycle. You will also practice making live calls with API key, product code, and authorization headers to secure sessions.

Next, you will see how the Go implementation is structured with the Gin framework. Routes such as teams connect to handlers that fetch tenant-scoped data, ensuring isolation in a multi-tenant system. You will learn how Gin serializes structs into clean, indented JSON and how the Status API organizes modular request/response handling. By the end, you will know how to define routes, process headers, connect to MongoDB, and return structured JSON, while adopting habits like hot reloading, tenant isolation, and client-oriented API design, a reusable template for your own microservices.

courses.name: Implementing Web Services in Ruby
courses.title: Let's take a quick look at implementing REST endpoints in Ruby. We'll go over routes, services, models and make some code changes to see how they take effect (Length: 22 minutes).
courses.description: Let's take a quick look at implementing REST endpoints in Ruby. We'll go over routes, services, models and make some code changes to see how they take effect. At the end of this 20-minute course, you should be able to start creating Web Services in Ruby. We'll pick one of the Ruby Frameworks we have a preference towards, but the learning should be agnostic to the framework.

descriptions: This course is a hands-on introduction to Ruby-based APIs, using our production services as context. In under 30 minutes, you will walk through real endpoints, explore the request/response cycle, and see how Ruby APIs support live apps. Starting with our Project Management platform, you will study two key endpoints: the dashboard, which aggregates data, and keys, which lists projects. Through diagrams and demos, you will trace calls from client to persistence, learning how Snowpal modularizes security checks and response formatting so developers can focus on endpoint logic.

The course then introduces Sinatra, the lightweight Ruby framework behind this API. Unlike Rails, Sinatra lets teams define structures, routes, and flows with maximum flexibility. You will see how Snowpal organizes nearly 700 endpoints while keeping exception handling and reusable functions consistent. The course also covers MongoDB integration, showing how the keys endpoint queries collections, applies filters, and sorts by last modified, with caching to boost performance. By the end, you will have a clear model of defining Ruby endpoints, connecting persistence, and returning structured responses.

courses.name: Update: Firebase Cloud Messaging
courses.title: Update your apps to reflect the latest Firebase Cloud Messaging APIs and SDKs (Length: 19 minutes).
courses.description: If you are using Google Firebase Cloud Messaging APIs and SDKs, you may have received an email recently asking you to update your apps to the latest versions of those APIs & SDKs. Google gives you a window of time before which you need to do this but it is better to take care of things like this sooner than later. There's at least 3 (maybe, 4) things you need to do, and in this course, we'll go over each of those steps with examples so it is easy enough for you to map it to your systems, and make the corresponding changes.

descriptions: This course provides a practical walkthrough of migrating from the Firebase Cloud Messaging legacy APIs to v1, based on real changes Snowpal made in production. You will see what the Google deprecation notice means, what breaks if ignored, and how to adapt before the June 2024 deadline. Though Snowpal runs largely on AWS, it uses Firebase for mobile push alerts that power collaboration. When teammates share blocks, pods, or messages, FCM ensures instant delivery to iOS and Android devices, showing why keeping integrations current is critical for reliable communication.

The biggest change is authentication: static API keys are replaced by short-lived OAuth 2.0 tokens from service account credentials. You will learn to download keys, configure them, and use Google auth libraries in Ruby or Node to fetch tokens. The course then covers payload updates where legacy fields must now be nested under a message object, with iOS and Android requiring different attributes. You will follow a systematic approach: start with a parent message, test locally, fix validation errors, and iterate. By the end, you will know how to update endpoints, restructure payloads, and modernize FCM reliably.

courses.name: Flutter App: Class Hierarchy (With A Working Example)
courses.title: Let's take a (fairly big) feature and understand what the class hierarchy looks like (Length: 31 minutes).
courses.description: The Snowpal Project Management App supports a Checklists feature that allows you to create any number of checklists, where you can add one or more checklist items. It has a number of actions associated with it, and is a pretty good example to take to help explain the Widget Class hierarchy. The idea, by the end of this course, is for you to have a good sense of what it takes to break a new feature requirement down into a class structure.

descriptions: This course explores structuring class hierarchies in Flutter through our production mobile app. Rather than abstract theory, you will see how a real feature is designed for clean, reusable, scalable code. The app supports project and task management across keys, blocks, and pods, with checklists central to breaking down work. You will study how checklists are modeled and integrated, starting with a BaseChecklist widget that handles titles, items, and sorting. From it, classes like KeyChecklist, BlockChecklist, PodChecklist, and BlockPodChecklist extend functionality while avoiding duplication.

The course also explores the functional side of checklists items, models, and services. You will see how class hierarchies connect to logic, how models represent data, and how services link UI to backend. The instructor explains how teams split responsibilities between presentation and functionality, coordinating via APIs and shared models. By the end, you will know how to balance inheritance and composition, organize base and specialized widgets, and integrate functional logic with presentation. The result is a blueprint for structuring scalable Flutter code that adapts as features grow.

courses.name: Vimeo + Canva: Add Edited Video to Showcase
courses.title: What does it take to publish an edited video to a showcase on Vimeo? (Length: 36 minutes)
courses.description: If you create video content regularly, there's a good chance you host it somewhere (or happen to be looking for a good place to host them). At Snowpal, we use videos for a variety of purposes and one of them relates to Snowpal Education where we create and publish courses for purchase (such as this one). We explored a few different ways to host these videos, and arrived at an approach that works best for us. In this course, we will go over that approach and walk you through OS X Final Cut Pro, Canva, Vimeo and DNSimple. We are confident that this will answer a few questions for you.

descriptions: This course walks you through publishing a video end to end, from an MP4 on your desktop to a polished showcase under a custom domain. You will start in Final Cut Pro, trimming, cropping, adjusting audio, filters, speed, and exporting properly while avoiding upload pitfalls. Next, you will use Canva to transform the raw file into a branded asset by adding backgrounds, logos, overlays, text, and audio tracks. The focus is on quick, practical edits that improve quality and engagement without requiring design expertise, giving you a streamlined process for producing shareable videos.

Next, you will upload to Vimeo, adding titles, descriptions, tags, and thumbnails while configuring privacy and access. You will learn to create showcases (Vimeo playlists) and organize videos into branded collections. The course then shows how to connect Vimeo showcases to a custom domain by configuring DNS records, setting up CNAMEs, and verifying access under your URL. This makes videos feel fully integrated with your brand. By the end, you will have a repeatable workflow: edit in Final Cut Pro, enhance in Canva, host in Vimeo, and publish under your own domain for a professional video presence.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.description: Edit a video on Final Cut Pro, create a new graphic on Canva, & upload it to Vimeo.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.description: Add record on DNS Provider, create showcase on Vimeo, and publish it.

courses.name: Flutter App: Directory Structure
courses.title: One of the first things you want to get out of your way when building a new App is the Directory Structure (Length: 40 minutes).
courses.description: Some frameworks dictate the directory structure to a large extent (hint: Rails!) but there are plenty others that give you all the leeway to structure it the way it works best for you. Flutter is one of them. While the flexibility is unquestionably desirable, it can (and does) act as a double edged sword. It is imperative that you get the structure (right) so it is intuitive to your team members as your team grows. In this course, we'll look at a Production Flutter App (our own Snowpal app) and review the directory structure that we arrived at (after a few iterations).

descriptions: This course walks through structuring the directory layout of a Flutter app, using our production codebase as a real-world example. Live in both app stores, it shows how large-scale apps stay maintainable and help new developers onboard quickly. You will learn why structure is critical early, how the freedom of Flutter contrasts with Rails conventions, and how smart choices save time. Lessons focus on the lib directory, where Snowpal organizes API integrations and UI code. The project management app showcases a layout supporting 400+ endpoints and features mirroring most of its web platform.

Next, the course explores the API directory design. Each resource keys, blocks, pods, comments, notifications maps to its own file, making endpoints easy to find and aligning product terminology with file names for consistency. A utility file centralizes network call logic, handling verbs, bodies, headers, and authorization so endpoint files stay clean. This abstraction reduces duplication and makes shifts, such as moving from REST to GraphQL, seamless. By the end, you will have a blueprint for structuring production ready Flutter apps that scale and help new engineers ramp up quickly.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.description: Define a directory structure for a Flutter App.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.description: Review every directory in Snowpal's Mobile App in some detail.

courses.name: Architect a Web Application
courses.title: There's many ways to architect a Web Application. Let's look at one of those ways (Length: 34 minutes).
courses.description: There's no one way to architect any application. With that said, some ways tend to work a tad better than others. In addition, the architecture of any application is bound to continually change as user base grows, as requirements change, as SLAs become tighter, as organizational structures change, and more. So, while it is important to get the architecture right to begin with, what's even more important is to ensure that it is resilient to change, is extensible, is flexible and long story short, stands the test of time. In this course, we'll look at one such architecture.

descriptions: This course walks through architecting a real world web app using our production system as the example. Instead of abstract theory, it shows how a project management app stable, performant, and used by thousands was built and scaled. You will start with a simple Ruby on Rails app connected to MongoDB, the foundation of our MVP, and learn its strengths and limits. Then you will see the shift from server side rendering to a single page app with Backbone.js, improving responsiveness, and how React was later adopted incrementally, proving teams can evolve stacks without full rewrites.

Next, the course shows how Snowpal separated business logic into dedicated backend services, moving work out of Rails controllers while keeping Rails as a proxy. This let front-end teams focus on UI/UX while backend teams specialized in logic, scaling, and integrations. You will then see the evolution to microservices, where services like content, conversations, and integrations own their databases and responsibilities. This modular approach boosts scalability, deployment safety, and team independence. By the end, you will have a blueprint for evolving from monolith to microservices with clear trade-offs.

courses.name: Integrate Kanban in Web Application
courses.title: it is likely you've used Kanban several times but may not have implemented one. So, this course should help (Length: 35 minutes).
courses.description: Kanban is an immensely popular way to schedule your activities. We'll take a look at implementing one. Our Web Application supports multiple rendering modes, one of which is a Kanban mode. There's a number of things you can do when you are in Kanban mode, and all of it is functionality we wired (read: handcoded) into a Kanban component that we integrated. Essentially, we started off with integrating a Kanban component (and yes, we never try to reinvent the wheel!), and added all the necessary functionality we needed into it. In this course, we'll show you some of those.

descriptions: This course walks through implementing a Kanban interface in a real production web app. Using our live system, you will learn not just how Kanban works but how to build it at scale. After reviewing the role of Kanban in workflows, you will see how Snowpal added it as a third view alongside list and tile modes. Then the course covers integrating Webix, explaining why the team licensed instead of building from scratch, how the base setup works, and how to adapt third-party libraries for production. You will gain practical insight into trade-offs, costs, and real integration challenges.

Next, the course dives into wiring functionality onto the Kanban UI. You will learn how to move tasks, link content, manage access, and share boards, with real code showing the base and the required customization. A key theme is separating presentation from behavior: extending base views, styling with CSS/Sass, and managing events with JavaScript or TypeScript. You will also pick up tips on experimenting with snippets before integrating into production. By the end, you will have a blueprint for adding Kanban to any app, with lessons on architecture, patterns, and pitfalls to avoid.

courses.name: Designing UI & UX for a New Feature on a Web App
courses.title: Let's take a look at a simple, new feature we are implementing on Snowpal Web App, and understand the development process (Length: 30 minutes).
courses.description: We implement new features (and enhancements) on a daily basis at Snowpal, and while how we approach each of those features from a UI/UX standpoint really depends, and is driven primarily by the feature and its complexities, there are many aspects of our approach that are generic to almost all features and enhancements. In this course, we'll take a look at a simple feature to help understand what the process looks like. We'll start with Requirements, discuss User Experience (UX), immediately followed by User Interface (UI). Note that we'll be focusing on a Web Application but a lot of what we learn would be just as applicable to Mobile Apps as well.

descriptions: This course offers a practical, end-to-end walkthrough of building a small web feature, showing how our team turns a request into a working solution in a single day. The example is a course list with filters, titles, descriptions, and purchase links. You will see how upfront planning shapes data needs, interactions, and priorities. Then the focus shifts to UX design: mapping requirements into flows, placing features for visibility, defining dropdown and search behavior, and shaping click actions. The course emphasizes speed, pragmatism, and iteration to deliver value quickly.

The course then explores UI options, weighing whether to extend a homegrown component, customize a licensed DHTMLX combo box, or use a modal with filtering. Each path is evaluated for speed, UX quality, and reuse, showing how Snowpal balances polish and delivery. A key theme is iteration: avoiding analysis paralysis by prototyping, testing in dev tools, and converging on the best fit. You will also learn to handle state, resets, and user expectations. By the end, you will have a blueprint for approaching small UI/UX features pragmatically and turning them into opportunities for improvement.

courses.name: Creating Products on AWS Marketplace
courses.title: If you are selling digital products, AWS Marketplace is one of those places you would be better served listing your products on (Length: 43 minutes).
courses.description: AWS Marketplace offers multiple categories for you to list your products under, one of which is SaaS. If you are looking to sell SaaS products, and are an AWS customer, I highly recommend that you list your products in the marketplace as it will provide plenty of visibility for you. In this course, I'll walk you through the process of listing a SaaS product on AWS Marketplace as it can be a tad overwhelming at times. We launched a number of API products recently, and I will be sharing that experience with you in this course. The aim is that by the end of this course, You will have a good sense of what it takes to list your products on the marketplace.

descriptions: This course walks through publishing digital products on AWS Marketplace using our real APIs. Instead of theory, it shows how to move from draft product to live listing customers can subscribe to. You will learn why SaaS vendors and API providers should list on Marketplace, from the trusted infra of AWS to its enterprise reach, and see how Snowpal distributes APIs like Building Blocks, Project Management, and Classroom. Lessons also cover pricing models subscription, contract, and consumption plus how to define units, tiers, and billing trade offs, with tips on constraints and upfront decisions.

Next, the course covers product creation in AWS Marketplace: setting up a SaaS listing, uploading assets, writing descriptions, choosing categories, and adding highlights. You will learn compliance steps like tax forms, bank details, and contracts, plus the value of logos, docs, and videos for discoverability. The course also shows how to design subscriber onboarding flows, since Marketplace lacks built-in support. Using our example, you will see how new customers get an API key and product code within minutes, while handling dev, staging, and production environments for a seamless experience.

courses.name: Authenticating Subscribers using API Key & Product Code
courses.title: You will need an API Key & Product Code to authenticate your API Requests. Let's look at the Why & the How (Length: 28 minutes).
courses.description: You will need to provide an API Key for you to authenticate your API Requests. There's many ways to generate this key and share it with your subscribers, and in this course, we'll look at one of those ways. In addition, you will likely also need to publish an API code to your subscribers if you have listed more than 1 SaaS Product (say, on the AWS Marketplace, or one of the many API Hubs). I'll walk you through our high level architecture so you can leave this course with a fair understanding of what it took us to support these 2 attributes (API Key & Product Code) in our implementation.

descriptions: In this course, you will learn how to generate, manage, and distribute API Keys to authenticate your API requests. We will explore one practical approach you can use to securely share keys with your subscribers. If you offer multiple SaaS products, and as a result list them on AWS Marketplace or any major API hub, then you may also need to publish a unique API Product Code. I will walk you through the high-level architecture behind our implementation so you will leave with a clear understanding of how we support both API Keys and Product Codes in a scalable, real-world environment.

The course also tackles multi-environment support, which hubs like AWS Marketplace do not provide natively. Snowpal solves this by provisioning separate products for dev, staging, and prod, each with its own API key and product code. You will see how this setup gives teams and subscribers sandbox flexibility. Using diagrams and Postman calls, the course shows how to send headers, structure requests, and use SDKs to simplify integration. By abstracting logic into libraries, you can shift between REST, GraphQL, or new environments seamlessly, ensuring secure, scalable authentication from day one.

courses.name: JSON Data Modeling: A Simple Example
courses.title: JSON is one of the most popular and commonly used formats for data exchange. Let's understand how it works (Length: 31 minutes).
courses.description: You can represent hierarchical data in many ways with one of the most popular formats being JSON. If you are a UI developer, you are likely consuming JSON Data, and if you are a server side engineer, you are providing JSON Data (via REST or Graph APIs, for instance). It is imperative that your JSON Schema looks accurate and is a true structural representation of the problem you are setting out to solve. If it isn't, it is surely going to cause a bit of pain as your product's adoptability grows (think backward compatibility, refactoring, extensibility, and more such challenges). In this course, we will take a recent feature we implemented on our Web App, and design the actual JSON Data Model alongside exploring alternative structures.

descriptions: This course introduces JSON data modeling through a real feature from our platform: representing course listings, previews, and metadata. You will learn when and why to use JSON as the contract between server, API, and client teams. Starting with basics like IDs, names, and short descriptions, the schema is expanded step by step to include details such as pricing, logos, thumbnails, and preview URLs. Along the way, you will see how to separate internal attributes (e.g., tags for search) from external ones (e.g., user-facing descriptions), building clean, extensible JSON for real-world apps.

The course highlights best practices for scalable, flexible JSON. You will learn to avoid brittle designs by replacing hardcoded labels with arrays, enabling features to grow without breaking clients. Topics include handling multi-currency pricing, structuring URLs for previews and chapters, and keeping schemas consistent across web and mobile. Collaboration is also emphasized: documenting JSON, saving DSLs alongside generated JSON, and using lightweight tools for iteration. By treating JSON as a contract agreed on in design reviews, you will gain a framework for building developer-friendly, future-proof schemas.

courses.name: SQL Vs NoSQL: Which Way to Go?
courses.title: A lot us have a sense of the basic differences but it continues to remain a question that, for some reason, doesn't seem easy enough to answer. Let's give it a shot (Length: 66 minutes).
courses.description: SQL (or RDBMS) has been around for a long time now. NoSQL databases are relatively newer but they too have been around for what feels like an eon now! Despite that, every time a new App, a new Service, or a new System is designed, there continues to be a sense of uncertainty around which direction to go (at least, it seems that way). There's a few reasons for that, and there's no single correct answer. So, while it surely depends on a variety of factors, and there is no dearth of documentation online about the differences between the 2 types of database systems, I still think it is worth a short course on it. In this hour-long course, we'll take another look at the database options available today, and try to determine which ones would make the most sense, and when.

descriptions: This course walks through the key differences between SQL and NoSQL, using real world examples to show why each design matters. You will start with SQL fundamentals schemas, primary keys, and relationships and see how they deliver consistency for transactional workloads like banking or e commerce. Then you will explore NoSQL types, including document, key value, wide column, and graph databases. Each is paired with use cases, from flexible content models to high speed lookups, highlighting the scalability and flexibility NoSQL provides. By the end, you will know how to choose the right approach for your app.

With foundations in place, the course moves to decision-making frameworks. You will weigh scalability, query complexity, schema evolution, and CAP theorem trade-offs. Examples show when to pick SQL for strong transactions versus NoSQL for high-volume, unstructured data. Best practices highlight pitfalls to avoid, like hardcoding SQL schemas or missing indexes in NoSQL, and strategies such as modeling with arrays or handling multi-currency pricing. The course closes with real scenarios, giving you the tools to design systems that are resilient today and adaptable for tomorrow.

courses.name: Flutter App: Implement Tabs
courses.title: While an app is bound to comprise many components, there are always a few components that are used a lot more frequently. Tabs happens to be one of them (Length: 18 minutes).
courses.description: Flutter as a Framework provides a rich set of components, thereby enabling you to focus on spending all your energies on your business requirements. So, even when you need to implement tabs, you have the choice of using the OOTB Flutter Tab Widget, or finding one that's a tad richer by going to (pub.dev). Snowpal's Mobile Apps are on the App and Play Stores, and while we've built a number of custom components, we refrain from doing it (or using a 3rd party plugin) unless we find significant value in doing so. As far as Tabs go, we are quite happy with what Flutter supports and all our tab implementations use the underlying Flutter Tab widgets. In this course, we'll look at one of our Tab Implementations where I'll walk you through our code so you get a sense of how tabs work in Flutter, and how you can easily leverage them.

descriptions: This hands on course shows how to build production quality tab navigation in Flutter using our live codebase. In 15 to 20 minutes, you will see how a simple, reliable tab interface ties complex features together while staying easy to extend. Starting in the dashboard flow, you will work with two anchor tabs Your Keys and System Keys to connect UI structure with product concepts like projects and boards. You will then explore Flutter components Scaffold, TabBar, Tab, TabController, and stateful widgets plus conventions like scoping, nesting, and private helpers to keep code clean and safe.

The course then dives into implementation details: initializing TabController in initState, setting defaults like redirecting to System Keys, handling onTap to refresh lists, update state, and toggle the floating action button. You will learn to use post-build callbacks for tasks such as scrolling to messages and dispose for cleanup. Third-party tab plugins are briefly reviewed, with guidance to start with the built-ins by Flutter and add polish only when it improves UX. By the end, you will have a reusable tab template that connects product concepts to UI primitives, keeping apps intuitive and production-ready.

courses.name: Asynchronous Messaging with RabbitMQ
courses.title: A quick look at how a production implementation of Asynchronous messaging with RabbitMQ works. At Snowpal, we use RabbitMQ quite heavily (till it is all ported over to Kafka, that is!) (Length: 45 minutes).
courses.description: What you do not need to do real time, you should try not to do real time for a variety of reasons. In this course, we'll look at a specific implementation that uses RabbitMQ as a Message Broker to better understand the pros and cons of various alternatives, including but not limited to whether or not you need to use messaging at all to solve such a problem. We'll touch upon Kafka a tiny, tiny bit but keep our focus primarily to Messaging Architecture in general, and RabbitMQ as a broker in particular. By the end of this course, you should be in a position to tell when you need to use a Message Broker, which one you may want to use, and how you should go about using it. While what we'll look at is a Ruby Microservice implementation, the learning would be just as applicable to other brokers and other languages.

descriptions: This course introduces asynchronous messaging with RabbitMQ, showing how Snowpal uses it in production to power real-time notifications and events. You will see how user actions like sharing content trigger notifications handled separately from core logic, making systems more reliable and scalable. A live block-sharing example illustrates the benefits of separation. The course then contrasts synchronous vs asynchronous design, showing how RabbitMQ decouples producers and consumers. By the end, you will understand why async messaging matters and how to implement it effectively in web and mobile apps.

Next, the course explores RabbitMQ architecture. You will see how messages move through exchanges and queues, with workers subscribing to specific tasks one for email, another for SMS, a third for in app notifications. Topics include distributed design, retries, fault tolerance, and dead letter queues. A Ruby based microservice example then shows how to configure RabbitMQ, set up publisher/subscriber channels, and build a base worker extended by specialized ones. By the end, you will know how to structure messaging services that separate concerns and scale reliably with growing traffic and complexity.

courses.name: Multi Tenant Architecture - Options
courses.title: A multi tenant architecture lets you serve many clients using a (single) instance of a software application. Do you ever wonder how your persistence layer should be architected in a multi tenant architecture? (Length: 50 minutes)
courses.description: We serve multiple clients via our Backend as a Service systems, and given that, multi tenancy is a core part of our architecture. While nothing is etched in stone and things are always subject to change, there are certain aspects of Software Architecture that, if you are not careful about, will be rather costly to make alterations to, and Multi Tenancy is definitely one of them. So, we explored several different options before arriving at the one we ended up implementing. When it comes to multi tenancy, there's at least 4 options available, and which one you should ideally go with depends on a variety of factors. In this course, we are going to take a deeper look at each of these 4 architectures and review their pros and cons. The objective is that by the end of this course, you will have a good understanding of multi tenancy, and therefore, will be in a slightly better position to evaluate your choices, and go with the one that makes the most sense for your organization.

descriptions: This course demystifies multi tenancy, showing how one application can securely serve many business customers. In 20 to 40 minutes, you will learn pragmatic patterns for structuring persistence so the data of each tenant is safe and scalable, with examples from our production systems. It starts by clarifying single instance as one deployable codebase across nodes, then frames multi tenancy as essential for B2B SaaS. You will compare four storage patterns schemas per tenant, databases per tenant, shared tables with tenant IDs, and tables per tenant evaluating pros, cons, and operational trade offs.

The course shows how shared tables can be secured with row-level security, shifting enforcement from queries to database policies and reducing leakage risk. Using Postgres and MongoDB, it maps patterns like per schema, per database, and shared collections across SQL and NoSQL, stressing that choices hinge on isolation, scale, and cost more than vendor. Grounded in our API platform on AWS Marketplace, it illustrates onboarding, default schema isolation, and when per-database models are offered. By the end, you will have a framework to choose and evolve the right multi-tenant design.

courses.name: Serverless Applications: AWS SAM Specification
courses.title: Understanding SAM Templates is key to seamlessly maneuvering AWS Serverless Applications (Length: 48 minutes).
courses.description: Serverless Applications have been around a bit, and it is hard to see any ecosystem in a company where they do not play a part. There is a lot to Serverless Apps so what we will do in this course is focus on what it takes to build AWS Server Applications using SAM Templates. SAM Templates are an extension of AWS CloudFormation Templates but are a whole lot easier to work with (at least, once you get the hang of it).

descriptions: This course introduces building serverless apps on AWS with SAM (Serverless Application Model) templates. You will see how Snowpal uses serverless functions and gateways to run APIs at scale, and why SAM simplifies infrastructure as code. Instead of hand coding CloudFormation, a few lines of YAML expand into hundreds of managed configs. After a Hello World demo, you will compare it to our production templates. The course then unpacks SAM anatomy Globals, Parameters, Resources, Outputs showing how to define APIs, Lambdas, DynamoDB tables, and permissions with real world examples.

The course stresses security, maintainability, and incremental growth. You will learn how IAM roles and managed policies regulate service access, why least privilege is critical, and how to structure templates by adding one resource at a time. Guidance covers balancing Lambda size, validating often, and reducing deployment risk. Beyond templates, you will use AWS CLI and SAM CLI, configure samconfig.toml, and run init, build, and deploy. By the end, you will know why SAM exists, how to scale from simple to production apps, and how to design serverless systems that are safe, reliable, and maintainable.

courses.name: Amazon DynamoDB: Introduction
courses.title: Amazon DynamoDB is a NoSQL database you want to familiarize yourself with, if you are an AWS user (Length: 48 minutes).
courses.description: If you work on Serverless Architectures, and are building Lambdas on AWS, it is highly likely you are already using DynamoDB, & if you are not, it is only a matter of time before you realize you really ought to. While there is no dearth of NoSQL databases, and despite the fact that AWS has plentiful support (to varying degrees) for a number of them, DynamoDB is a slightly unique database and it has a specific purpose when it comes to where it fits in & how well it does. Given that, it is certainly useful to understand it a bit (better).

descriptions: This course offers a fast, practical intro to Amazon DynamoDB, aimed at both newcomers to AWS and those seeking production-tested guidance. You will learn when DynamoDB fits as a managed NoSQL store and how Snowpal uses it with Lambda and API Gateway. Lessons map SQL terms (tables, records, columns) to DynamoDB tables, items, and attributes, then cover partition and sort keys, composite keys, and data types. You will set up with AWS CLI, DynamoDB console, NoSQL Workbench, and DynamoDB Local in Docker, gaining hands-on experience plus tips for debugging and managing local vs cloud workflows.

The course then covers core DynamoDB operations with real examples. You will create tables, put and update items, and compare queries (keyed lookups) with scans (full table scans with filters). You will write PartiQL, avoid pitfalls like quoting errors, and see how projections and filters impact cost. Next, you will model for flexibility with Global and Local Secondary Indexes, exploring service limits and non-key access patterns. You will also use DynamoDB Streams to trigger Lambdas. The course closes by showing DynamoDB in a serverless stack, leaving you ready to model keys and build workflows.

courses.name: LIVE Coding: Implement Notifications Feature
courses.title: Let us make some changes to an existing Ruby API, and do it LIVE (Length: 95 minutes).
courses.description: Let us implement a feature in this course. A real feature. As in, one that will be deployed to Production shortly, and be available on our Mobile Apps on the App and Play Stores. Here is what we will do. Add API support for a new type of notification so it is part of the Endpoint Response. Most importantly, we will do it together. You will see in real time how one could go about implementing a requirement from start to finish. You will get a feel of a few different tools & technologies (RubyMine IDE, MongoDB Client, REST API, and more).

descriptions: This course gives a live, end to end view of how our engineers ship a real feature. Instead of polished demos, you will follow actual service side development, seeing the trade offs and adjustments made in real time. It starts with a kickoff framing a scoped, practical enhancement sized for quick release, emphasizing clarity, defaults, and incremental delivery. Most of the course is live coding building routes, handlers, validations, and integrations while also showing unscripted steps like reading errors, testing assumptions, and revising approaches to keep momentum without losing quality.

To keep learning manageable, the course is split into an intro, one or two implementation sessions, and a recap mirroring the rhythm of a sprint planning, building, and reviewing. This pacing lets you code alongside with natural pause points. Along the way, you will pick up patterns like isolating changes behind clean APIs, shaping server responses for UI needs, and scoping features to stay shippable. You will also see tactics for short feedback loops: small runs, targeted logs, and quick validations. A closing debrief reviews what was built and refined, giving you a repeatable delivery approach.

courses.name: Social Media Login (OAuth 2.0)
courses.title: Adding support for multiple social media sign ins is pretty much an implicit requirement these days (Length: 56 minutes).
courses.description: If you are building an app today, it is likely you support some form of Social Media login. Or, if you are like us, you want to support all the most popular alternatives available: Facebook, Google, Apple and Microsoft. In addition, you may need to support sign in using one of these Social Media account both on Web and Mobile. If so, this course should help you. We will walk you through each of the 4 social media sign ins we support on Snowpal, both on Web and Mobile. This way, when the time comes to integrate one or more of these authentication mechanisms into your systems, you will not have to scramble for help.

descriptions: This course is a practical guide to implementing social logins with OAuth 2.0, using our production apps as examples. You will see how Facebook, Google, Apple, and Microsoft flows are integrated across web, iOS, and Android. After covering OAuth basics and why social login improves adoption and security, the course shows what to register with each provider, which credentials you need, and how redirect URIs return tokens to your app. Using real screenshots, you will create apps in Google, Facebook, Apple, and Microsoft portals, generate IDs and secrets, and configure URIs for dev, staging, and prod.

Next, the course covers application-side integration. In our Rails app, Devise and OmniAuth handle provider callbacks; you will configure routes, build controllers, and unify payloads into a consistent user model despite field differences. The course then shifts to mobile, showing how our Flutter app reuses the same OAuth flows with mobile SDKs and redirect patterns. You will learn to adapt concepts across platforms for seamless sign-in. By the end, you will know how to configure providers, wire flows in backend and frontend, and apply production-ready patterns for major social logins.

courses.name: RevenueCat: Pricing Integration
courses.title: Pricing is not a feature your customers are necessarily looking forward to! But, you still need it (Length: 46 minutes).
courses.description: Can you implement pricing on mobile without using any 3rd party (intermediary) plugins? Absolutely. Should you do that (though)? Maybe. Maybe not. Let us take a look at why RevenueCat (or something like it) would make a meaningful difference to development. We explored a few different options before choosing RevenueCat, and we are happy with that decision (at least, so far!).

descriptions: This course is a practical guide to implementing in-app purchases and subscriptions in mobile apps, using our production experience. You will learn to set up flows with Apple App Store, Google Play, and intermediaries like RevenueCat, and see why abstraction simplifies scaling. The course compares direct store SDK integration with the RevenueCat wrapper, highlighting complexity, compatibility issues, and maintenance trade-offs. You will then explore the app-side UX for purchases and subscriptions, covering consumables, non-consumables, and recurring plans, and how UIs adapt after purchase or restore on iOS and Android.

The course then examines pricing architecture, contrasting direct store integration with flows using RevenueCat as a layer between your app and the App Store or Play Store. You will also see how to sync purchases with your backend or our APIs. Implementation is shown with Flutter code: configuring store connections, using API keys, creating offerings, and managing entitlements. You will validate purchases, restore subscriptions, and control premium access with concise examples. By the end, you will know how to set up products, integrate RevenueCat, test on devices, and plan for long-term maintainability.

courses.name: Dependencies in Development Environment
courses.title: If you know the roads, driving becomes easier. It is no different when it comes to dev environments & dependencies (Length: 40 minutes).
courses.description: What are your dependencies in your dev environment, and how easy is it to switch your dependencies? Most of us love to do a lot of our work locally for productivity reasons but there are times you need to connect to other systems even in your lowest environment (your developer machine). Let us take a real world example and see how that works in a product company.

descriptions: This course gives a behind the scenes view of how engineering teams set up and manage dev environments. Using our real workflows, it shows how apps are built, debugged, and shipped from local development to production scale deployments. Starting with a Rails web app, you will run locally, connect to a database, test endpoints, and iterate in the browser. Lessons then expand to team scenarios with shared databases and collaboration trade offs. As products grow, you will see how microservices layer in, each with its own APIs and dependencies, and how developers balance speed with accuracy.

The course next covers multiple environments dev, test, staging, and prod showing how the same service connects to different databases by context. You will see why some bugs must be reproduced in staging and how to minimize downtime when switching. External dependencies are also explored, from Kafka and RabbitMQ to Snowpal APIs and Stripe, with guidance on wiring, sandboxes, and scripts to spin them up quickly. By the end, you will know how to navigate new environments, choose essential dependencies, rely on shared setups when needed, and avoid overcomplicating local workflows.

courses.name: Interfaces in Go (Golang)
courses.title: What are interfaces in Go? And how are they different from interfaces in other languages? (Length: 55 minutes)
courses.description: According to Golang documentation, an interface type is defined as a set of method signatures. Fair enough, and that sounds like it is quite similar to how interfaces work in other languages. While there certainly are similarities, there are also nuances that you would be better served understanding before leveraging this construct. In this course, we will take a simple example (a manufactured one, sure) to understand how interfaces work in Go, and do a bit of LIVE coding. The idea is that by the end of this course, you will have a good sense of how interfaces work, and when they may be a good fit for the problem you are trying to solve.

descriptions: This course is a hands on introduction to interfaces in Go, showing not just what they are but why they matter in real projects. Through live coding, you will see interfaces emerge naturally while solving problems instead of abstract definitions. It starts with a restaurant example serving food and drinks, where you will define interfaces and implement them in structs step by step. Then lessons expand into structs, methods, and receivers creating Food, Drink, and Dessert types with Serve methods and show how implicit conformance within Go lets structs satisfy interfaces without explicit declarations.

The example expands to provisioning deciding if an order is delivered or picked up. You will write methods for conditions like delivery distance, implement multiple interfaces (Serve, Provision), and pass them into higher level functions, showing separation of concerns. Krish stresses keeping implementations small, testing often, and using interfaces to decouple logic so new types fit without rewrites. Adding a Dessert type proves it one method makes it work with existing functions. By the end, you will know how Go interfaces differ, and how they make code modular, extensible, and maintainable.

courses.name: Develop AWS Lambda Applications locally
courses.title: Too often, I see good developers wait on deployments that take minutes to test their changes. There are better ways. (Length: 32 minutes)
courses.description: If you are thinking about building Serverless Functions, there is a high chance you are thinking about AWS Lambda. They have been around a long time. They are fairly easy to build but the one thing I have seen developers do repeatedly is rely on a deployment to the Cloud before they test their changes. There is more optimal ways. Let us discuss one of them.

descriptions: This course tackles a key AWS Lambda challenge: testing and iterating without redeploying every change to the cloud. While Lambda is central to modern architectures, deployment cycles add costly delays. Using our production APIs as examples, you will see how Lambdas integrate into real systems and where deploy to test workflows fall short. A live demo with AWS SAM shows the time lost during repeated deployments, underscoring why local workflows matter not to skip deployment, but to code faster and only push when features are ready for integration or review.

Next, you will learn our solution: a local pass-through that mimics Lambda without leaving your machine. An Express app proxies requests, maps them into Lambda event objects, and invokes the same handler logic as production. You will hot-reload changes and test instantly in Postman. Step by step, the course shows wiring routes for all HTTP verbs, building event objects, and handling local dependencies like DynamoDB. Clear diagrams explain where simulation stops and why final tests must run in AWS. By the end, you will have a repeatable workflow balancing speed with accuracy for Lambda dev.

courses.name: Writing scripts to understand REST APIs
courses.title: Developers like to review API documentation slightly differently. They prefer to use scripts. Let us write one then (in Golang). (Length: 34 minutes)
courses.description: If you are building integrations, or leverage other API Providers to reduce your Time to Market, you are bound to consume a fair number of APIs. When you do that, how quickly your team wraps their head around a brand new API is going to make all the difference between going LIVE in the next sprint vs one down the road. We use a simple tool that we created for one part of this purpose. Let us explore it.

descriptions: This course helps developers and product managers quickly consume large APIs without drowning in hundreds of endpoints or endless Postman clicks. Using our APIs, it shows how to go beyond docs by leveraging scripts and visuals to speed onboarding. You will see why Postman and OpenAPI alone can overwhelm, and how flattening and visualizing endpoints accelerates learning. Lessons walk through a Go based repo that processes Postman collections into clean Markdown, which is then converted into visual mind maps giving teams a single page, scannable view of every endpoint and verb.

The course next covers workflows like filtering endpoints by keyword, narrowing by HTTP verb, and merging multiple APIs into one view. These techniques help PMs gauge scope, let devs split tasks, and cut manual exploration. You will also see how outputs can auto-generate Jira or GitHub tickets for faster DevOps. Step-by-step, the course shows working with Postman exports, generating structs from JSON, and iterating on scripts that teams can extend. By the end, you will know how to onboard APIs in hours, explore visually, and reduce friction in the first step of integration.

courses.name: Get Started with Trading Stocks
courses.title: Learn the basics of trading. If you are looking to become an investor and are wary of the associated risks, this course should help you build your confidence. (Length: 53 minutes)
courses.description: Starting to trade and invest at a young age will help you achieve your financial goals in the long run. Even if you are someone who has done a bit of trading but are unsure about some of the terminologies and risks associated with trading, you will likely find value in this first course. We will publish more Finance courses in future where we will be discussing a variety of related topics, and this first course is meant to serve as the foundation for the rest to follow. In this course, we will help you understand the basics of investing (how much to invest, when to invest, why to invest, how to invest and so on).

descriptions: Trading 101 is a beginner-friendly guide to investing, emphasizing why starting young builds long-term success. You will learn how compounding, discipline, and early experience shape financial growth, while exploring core concepts like inflation, risk tolerance, and healthy money habits. The course then shifts to practical steps: how much to invest, where funds should come from, and why not to risk everyday money. You will also try paper trading with virtual cash to practice strategies and build confidence before using real capital, giving you a safe on-ramp into the stock market.

Next, you will learn how to choose a trading platform, comparing brokers like Fidelity and E-Trade, opening an account, and evaluating web and mobile tools. You will see why usability matters and how to match platforms to your style. The course then covers core strategies: diversification vs concentration, long- vs short-term trading, and dollar-cost averaging. You will explore balancing risk, using index funds or stocks, and tax basics like realized vs unrealized gains. By the end, you will grasp trading fundamentals and set realistic goals, building a foundation for more advanced courses ahead.

courses.name: Stocks: Buy, Sell, Short, Cover
courses.title: We will do a few different types of trades in this course by taking a hands-on approach. If you are a newbie, you are likely to benefit from it immensely. That said, it should help investors with some experience as well. (Length: 54 minutes)
courses.description: In this course, we will take a look at some of the common types of trades (and maybe, a little beyond them as well). We will pick a platform to trade (and do some paper trades), select some securities to perform a few different types of trades on, and see how goes. If you have not done any trading, or have done a little but not a whole not, this course should help answer a few questions.

descriptions: Trading 102 builds on Trading 101 by moving from concepts to execution. Using E-Trade platform, you will focus on paper trades to practice safely without real risk. After a refresher on why paper trading matters, the course introduces core trade types: buying, selling, shorting, and covering, with emphasis on their different risk exposures. You will then see how to place orders in E-Trade, starting with market orders that execute immediately and limit orders that wait for your target price. These live demos give you the mechanics and context needed to prepare for more advanced order types.

Next, you will dive into short selling selling stocks you do not own, why covering completes the trade, and why losses can exceed your investment. Examples highlight the risks and why many traders use caution. The course then introduces stop orders and trailing stops for risk management. You will see how stop loss and stop limit orders protect against downside, while trailing stops move with the market to lock in profits. By the end, you will be ready to execute basic and intermediate trades buying, selling, shorting, covering, and using stops building confidence with paper trading before going live.

courses.name: Stocks: Find the best companies to invest in
courses.title: Curious what a PE ratio is? Or what the difference between that and a PEG ratio is? Which one should you go with? (Length: 66 minutes)
courses.description: We will take a look at some of the ways to find the best companies to invest (both short term and long term). This, in itself, is a broad topic and not something we can cover in an hour but the idea is to equip you with necessary knowledge and awareness to get started. We will review PE Ratio, PEG Ratio, EBITDA, and more.

descriptions: Trading 103 builds on 101 and 102 by moving from trade mechanics to company analysis and diversification. You will learn key financial ratios P/E, PEG, EPS, and EBITDA explained simply and applied to real companies to show what strong or weak numbers signal about growth potential. The course also introduces research tools beyond trading accounts, such as Seeking Alpha, YCharts, TipRanks, and MarketWatch, and shows how to use their data to evaluate companies effectively. By the end, you will have the analytical tools to make more informed investment decisions and broaden your trading skills.

Diversification is a key focus of Trading 103. You will see how concentrating in one stock compares to spreading capital across industries, and how diversification reduces risk while over diversification may limit returns. Lessons use real companies Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, NVIDIA, Chipotle, Walmart, McDonald’s to show how different sectors balance a portfolio. By the end, you will know how to interpret ratios, use research tools, and judge whether stocks are fairly valued. Trading 103 builds the analytical mindset to move beyond mechanics and toward strategic, long term investing.

courses.name: Stocks: Portfolio Management
courses.title: Creating portfolios is not particularly hard but doing it efficiently can make all the difference between a profitable trade and a losing one as a day trader. (Length: 67 minutes)
courses.description: We discussed ratios in the last course and in this one, we will take a look at managing portfolios, understand the differences to investment as a Day Trader vs an Investor, and also, take a look at a few different charts. There are a number of public companies and selecting a handful to invest in can be rather challenging without the right set of tools so we will take a look at a few tools.

descriptions: Trading 104 continues the series with a focus on portfolio management. Building on trade mechanics, ratios, and diversification, this course teaches you how to structure, track, and manage investments. A key theme is comparing day traders who chase short-term swings with long-term investors focused on fundamentals and growth. You will explore the trade-offs between risk, reward, and time horizon. Hands-on lessons use tools like Seeking Alpha, YCharts, TipRanks, and BarChart to build sample portfolios, set watchlists, track holdings, and simulate trades with organized views and metrics.

This course also dives deeper into charts and data. You will learn to read intraday moves, analyze growth percentages, price swings, and volume trends, with examples from Apple, NVIDIA, McDonalds, and Sweetgreen to compare volatility, growth, and stability. The course explains margin trading how borrowing magnifies gains and losses, what margin calls mean, and why leverage requires strict risk management. By the end, you will know how to build and evaluate portfolios, balance trading vs investing strategies, and use research tools to shape decisions and align with your financial goals.

courses.name: Weaviate: Open Source Vector Database
courses.title: Weaviate is an open source AI-native database, and is one I stumbled into recently. (Length: 90 minutes)
courses.description: If you are building AI Applications, you should consider leveraging Vector Databases as they bring a lot of specific value to the table. In this course, we will learn a bit about Vector Databases taking Weaviate as an example, and do a tiny bit of hands on work.

descriptions: This course introduces Weaviate, an open source vector database built for unstructured data like text, images, and audio. By storing embeddings in high dimensional space, Weaviate powers semantic search, recommendations, and clustering capabilities beyond relational or NoSQL systems. You will start with embedding fundamentals and vector search, anchored by practical examples. Then you will set up a cloud cluster, configure authentication, and generate API keys. Using Go and Python clients, you will connect to Weaviate, validate the environment, and troubleshoot common issues like dependency mismatches or misconfigured endpoints.

Next, the course covers data modeling and ingestion. You will define schemas, choose vectorizers like OpenAI, and batch-ingest JSON datasets, verifying inserts via console and code. With data loaded, you will use GraphQL for semantic search, compare vectorizers such as OpenAI and Cohere, and weigh when to bring your own embeddings. Lessons highlight trade-offs in performance, accuracy, and cost, plus scaling strategies for collections and infrastructure. By the end, you will have set up Weaviate, ingested data, run queries, and gained a clear model for applying vector search in production use cases.

courses.name: Running a SaaS Business
courses.title: Do you ever dream of becoming an entrepreneur? Is that something you've wanted to do for a while but need a tiny bit of help getting started? (Length: 80 minutes)
courses.description: As someone who has always wanted to be an entrepreneur and as someone who decided to quit a stable, full time job to do this, I can share a few things with you that might help you in your own journey. Over the years, I have learned plenty and while there is a lot more to learn, I feel like I can share some of my experiences with you so you make fewer mistakes than I did.

descriptions: This course offers a functional roadmap to starting and running a SaaS business, from idea to product in customers hands. You will define the problem, audience, and execution strategy, test differentiation, and learn why momentum beats perfection. Explore funding options, runway, lifestyle choices, and cost management. Assess your skills, build a lean team across engineering, product, and sales, balance equity and pay, and decide on remote, onsite, or hybrid setups while fostering collaboration and trust.

This course offers a practical guide to starting and running a SaaS business from idea to launch. You will define the problem, target audience, and differentiation, learning why momentum beats perfection. Money and time come next: compare bootstrapping vs funding, estimate runway, adjust lifestyle, and stretch dollars. On skills and team, you will assess strengths, fill gaps, and build a lean core team across engineering, product, and sales. Lessons cover balancing equity with salary, hiring with limited resources, and choosing onsite, remote, or hybrid setups for collaboration and trust.

courses.name: How to Research Stocks
